source: Translating Between Motion Graphs
Turn an x–t graph into v–t and a–t graphs, and back again.
Students copy the shape of one graph onto the next instead of tracking slopes.

You can now read slopes on an x–t graph and slopes and areas on a v–t graph. Put those together and any one motion graph lets you sketch the other two. This is one of the most useful skills in mechanics, and one of the most often missed.
Going down the chain $x \to v \to a$, take slopes: the value of each graph is the slope of the one above it. Going up $a \to v \to x$, add up areas, starting from the known initial value.

Velocity is the rate of change of position, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. A rate of change is a slope. Undoing a slope means adding up small changes, and adding up a rate times small time steps is an area. So the three graphs are linked by the same two moves every time.
Four stages: speed up, cruise, slow to a stop, back up. The shapes of the three graphs are all different.
Read across a row: each graph is the slope of the one to its left.
Worked examples
An $x$–$t$ graph is a straight line rising from $x = 0$ to $x = 6\ \text{m}$ over $0$–$3\ \text{s}$, then flat until $t = 5\ \text{s}$. Sketch the $v$–$t$ graph.
From x to v
$v = 2\ \text{m/s}$ for $0$–$3\ \text{s}$, then $v = 0$.
First piece: slope $= \dfrac{6}{3} = 2\ \text{m/s}$, so $v$ is a flat line at $2\ \text{m/s}$ from $0$ to $3\ \text{s}$.
Second piece: slope $0$, so $v$ is a flat line on the axis from $3$ to $5\ \text{s}$.
The $v$ graph is a step down, not a copy of the ramp-then-flat shape.
A $v$–$t$ graph rises from $0$ to $6\ \text{m/s}$ during $0$–$2\ \text{s}$, stays at $6\ \text{m/s}$ until $5\ \text{s}$, then falls to $0$ at $8\ \text{s}$. Sketch the $a$–$t$ graph.
From v to a
$a = 3$, then $0$, then $-2\ \text{m/s}^2$.
Slopes: $\dfrac{6}{2} = 3\ \text{m/s}^2$, then $0$, then $\dfrac{-6}{3} = -2\ \text{m/s}^2$.
The $a$ graph is three flat pieces: $+3$, $0$, $-2\ \text{m/s}^2$.
Starting at $x = 0$, a cart has $v = 4\ \text{m/s}$ for $2\ \text{s}$, then $v = 0$ for $2\ \text{s}$, then $v = -2\ \text{m/s}$ for $3\ \text{s}$. Describe the $x$–$t$ graph.
From v up to x
Up to $8\ \text{m}$, flat, then down to $2\ \text{m}$.
Each piece changes $x$ by its area: $+8\ \text{m}$, then $0$, then $-6\ \text{m}$.
So $x$ climbs in a straight line to $8\ \text{m}$, stays flat, then falls in a straight line to $2\ \text{m}$.
Practice: which v–t graph matches? (B: the slopes are 2, 0 and −2 m/s. A copies the shape, C has the signs flipped, and D plots the positions instead of the slopes.)

Copying the shape of one graph onto the next. A ramp on the $x$ graph becomes a flat line on the $v$ graph, and a curve on the $x$ graph becomes a sloped line on the $v$ graph. Check each piece by asking "what is the slope here?" (going down) or "what area builds up here?" (going up), never "what does it look like?"
